summary.en: The crew of Japan Airlines cargo flight 1628 reported unusual lights over Alaska in November 1986. FAA records document the interviews and checks, but the agency said it could not confirm another aircraft or object.

bg: Екипажът на товарния полет на Japan Airlines съобщава за светлини над Аляска на 17 ноември 1986 г. FAA събира записи от разговори, интервюта с екипажа и материали за радарните проверки. Историческите файлове позволяват да се сравнят първоначалните твърдения и официалният анализ.

Екипажът на товарния полет JAL 1628 описва необичайни светлини по време на полет над Аляска. Тъй като историята се отнася до гражданска авиация, важно място заемат материалите на FAA: разговори със службите за контрол, интервюта и оценки на съответните радарни данни. Тези записи позволяват да се сравни какво са съобщили пилотите в момента на събитието и как е интерпретирано по-късно.

Официалната кореспонденция не потвърждава категорично друг летателен апарат или неизвестен обект. Оттук не следва, че свидетелите непременно са се заблудили; означава, че наличните независими данни не са достатъчни за окончателно заключение. За читателя най-полезни са времевите последователности, формулировките на екипажа и разликата между установено радарно наблюдение и предполагаема причина.
en: The Japan Airlines cargo crew reported lights over Alaska on November 17, 1986. FAA files include communications, interviews and radar-related investigation records. The historical documents let readers compare the original accounts with the official analysis.

The Japan Airlines cargo crew described unusual lights during a flight over Alaska. Because the report arose in civil aviation, the FAA records are particularly important: communications with air-traffic services, interviews and reviews of relevant radar information. These records help distinguish what the crew reported at the time from interpretations published afterward.

The official correspondence does not conclusively confirm another aircraft or unknown object. That is not proof that the crew fabricated or misperceived its experience; it means the independent evidence available in the documents is insufficient for a final identification. The most useful reading method is to compare the timeline, the crew's own wording and the difference between a recorded radar return and an inferred explanation.

en: Source-linked case dossier · disclosure.zone (CC BY 4.0). Date and location are taken from this independent catalog; map coordinates, if present, are approximate reference points.

Lights in a Norwegian valley and the volunteer field campaign of 1984: 188 reports, 36 radar recordings, three of them together with a light, and a report that says it did not find out what the phenomenon is

Unknown lights began to show up in the Hessdalen valley in December 1981. With no state institution taking it up, five people set up Project Hessdalen, and from 21 January to 26 February 1984 its volunteers watched the valley with cameras and spectral gratings, a radar, a spectrum analyser, a magnetometer, a seismograph, a laser, Geiger counters and infrared viewers, helped by the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment and universities. Of 188 reports, 135 were put down to known lights; the radar made 36 recordings, three of them probably of a light that was also seen. The report, signed by Erling Strand on 5 January 1985, concludes: “We have not found out what this phenomenon is.”

Source assessment: None. The 1984 campaign was a volunteer project, which its report says began because “no official institutes with governmental support seemed to care about these unknown lights”. Its conclusion: “We have not found out what this phenomenon is. That could hardly be expected either. But we know that the phenomenon, whatever it is, can be measured.”

Reported alternative 1: Known lights. The report put 135 of the 188 reports under “A known light”, 86 of them reports on planes, and wrote that a direct line to the radar station covering the district would have let the project pick out the planes. Where a known light ends and an unknown one begins was the authors’ own call: “It is therefore a subjective decision, but it is made by two persons.”

Reported alternative 2: Electrical charges from the ground, as a geophysical paper of 2024 suggests. Conductive zones “mainly related to mineral deposits (mainly sulfides)” trace a ring along a gabbro intrusion in the valley; strong electric fields rising from them, with gas such as radon, could produce lights by ionisation. Its authors call it “a provisional mechanism”.

Reported alternative 3: Movements in the ground, the reason the campaign set up a seismograph. The 1984 report: “Until now, we have not found any connection between the phenomenon and movements in the ground.” The 2024 paper says of the stress-driven version that seismicity in the valley “is so weak that this hypothesis cannot be retained”.
Reported alternative 4: An unknown phenomenon. The 1984 report: “We have not found out what this phenomenon is.”

summary.en: On 8 January 1981, at about 5 pm, a man working on a terrace behind his house in the Var saw a craft come down, rest on the ground for a few seconds and leave. Next morning he showed his wife the marks; neighbours alerted the gendarmerie, which photographed two concentric circles 2.20 and 2.40 m across and took samples. GEPAN, the group at the French space agency CNES that studied such reports, published the case in March 1983 as technical note no. 16. Its laboratories found the soil compacted and heated to no more than 600°, and Dr M. Bounias of INRA found pigment losses in wild alfalfa that were greater nearer the trace. GEPAN concluded that the interpretations were “trop diverses et vagues” (too varied and vague) to confirm the witness’s account, and that whether the plant changes matched his description “reste à savoir” (remains to be seen).

One witness, a ring pressed into a terrace in the Var, and GEPAN’s technical note no. 16: laboratories that found the ground marked and the plants altered, and a conclusion that could not tie either to the witness’s craft

On 8 January 1981, at about 5 pm, a man working on a terrace behind his house in the Var saw a craft come down, rest on the ground for a few seconds and leave. Next morning he showed his wife the marks; neighbours alerted the gendarmerie, which photographed two concentric circles 2.20 and 2.40 m across and took samples. GEPAN, the group at the French space agency CNES that studied such reports, published the case in March 1983 as technical note no. 16. Its laboratories found the soil compacted and heated to no more than 600°, and Dr M. Bounias of INRA found pigment losses in wild alfalfa that were greater nearer the trace. GEPAN concluded that the interpretations were “trop diverses et vagues” (too varied and vague) to confirm the witness’s account, and that whether the plant changes matched his description “reste à savoir” (remains to be seen).

Source assessment: GEPAN, technical note no. 16 (March 1983): the possible interpretations of the soil analyses “restent cependant trop diverses et vagues pour que l’on puisse considérer qu’elles fournissent une confirmation définitive des narrations du témoin” (remain too varied and vague to be taken as a definitive confirmation of the witness’s accounts); of the plant results, “Reste à savoir si cela correspond bien à la description fournie par le témoin” (it remains to be seen whether this matches the description the witness gave). A later CNES brochure on SEPRA: “Ce cas reste l’un des rares phénomènes inexpliqués dans les annales du SEPRA” (this case remains one of the few unexplained phenomena in SEPRA’s records). GEIPAN’s own page on the case could not be opened: its server refused requests (429).

Reported alternative 1: A blow or a rub by something heavy, which the laboratories describe without saying what it was. Metz: the black particles “semblent être des résidus de combustion” (seem to be combustion residues). Pau: the zinc and phosphate could come “d’une peinture noire primaire à base de Carbon black” (from a black primer paint based on carbon black). SNEAP found no organic compounds characteristic of the combustion products of hydrocarbon engines. GEPAN: such interpretations, “(choc, frottement...)” (impact, friction), remain “trop diverses et vagues” (too varied and vague).

Reported alternative 2: A helicopter. Asked by GEPAN about air traffic, the region’s civil and military authorities reported, after an inquiry by the ALAT, only an Alouette II flying over the area “à une hauteur de 200 m du sol aux environs de 16h.30 locales” (at 200 m above the ground at about 4:30 pm local time). The note records this and goes no further; the witness himself ruled out a helicopter because the craft was almost on the wall of the terrace.

Reported alternative 3: An unknown phenomenon that left the trace, as the witness described it. GEPAN: “Reste à savoir si cela correspond bien à la description fournie par le témoin” (it remains to be seen whether this matches the description the witness gave).

bg: Американски военнослужещи от RAF Woodbridge съобщават за светлини край Рендълшъм през декември 1980 г. Меморандумът на полк. Чарлз Холт е съхранен в британския Национален архив. По-късна кореспонденция и интервюта предлагат допълнителни, понякога различаващи се версии.

Случаят е свързан с разкази на американски военнослужещи край британските бази RAF Woodbridge и Bentwaters. Той е особено интересен заради наличието на съвременна на събитията служебна кореспонденция, включително известния меморандум на Чарлз Холт. Архивният документ показва, че съобщенията са били записани, но не е равнозначен на независимо потвърждение на всички по-късни детайли в свидетелските истории.

През годините около случая се появяват различни реконструкции и допълнителни интервюта. За надеждно изследване е важно да се отдели казаното непосредствено след случката от по-късните спомени и интерпретации. Сравнявай датите на документите, обстановката в района и възможните обичайни източници на светлина. Оставяме оценката отворена там, където източниците не са достатъчни.
en: US personnel from RAF Woodbridge reported lights near Rendlesham in December 1980. Lieutenant Colonel Charles Halt's memorandum is held by the UK National Archives. Later correspondence and interviews provide additional, sometimes differing accounts.

The accounts concern American service personnel near the RAF Woodbridge and Bentwaters installations in the United Kingdom. This case is notable for contemporary official correspondence, including Charles Halt's memorandum. That archival document demonstrates that reports were recorded; it does not by itself independently confirm every detail added in later witness accounts.

Several reconstructions and further interviews have appeared over the years. A careful investigation separates statements made close to the event from memories and interpretations recorded much later. Document dates, local conditions and potential ordinary light sources are central to comparing the competing explanations. Where the archival record does not settle a question, the dossier leaves it unresolved.

Операция „Плато“ включва военен интерес към сведения за светлини и необичайни преживявания в щата Пара, Бразилия, през 1977–1978 г. Събраните материали съдържат различни видове сведения — описания, фотографски материали и скици. Степента на надеждност не е еднаква за всяко от тях, затова досието не обединява всички разкази в едно потвърдено физическо събитие.

При преглед на архива е полезно да се проверят мястото, датата, авторът и обстоятелствата около всеки документ. Един архивен набор може да бъде голям, без това да означава, че всяка страница потвърждава отделно наблюдение. В AURORA разграничаваме свидетелски сведения, оригинални архивни документи и заключения, направени по-късно от изследователи.
en: In 1977–78 Brazilian military investigators collected testimony, photographs and sketches of lights in Pará. Surviving operation records include locations, times and descriptions.
Explore the original documents and testimony through the links below, including recordings and images where the publisher has released them.

Operation Saucer, or Operação Prato, involved military interest in reports of lights and unusual experiences in the Brazilian state of Pará during 1977–1978. The surviving material includes different kinds of sources: descriptions, photographs and sketches. These do not all carry equal evidential weight, so the dossier does not combine every account into a single confirmed physical event.

When reviewing the archival collection, readers should look for the location, date, author and circumstances of each document. A large document collection does not mean that every page verifies a separate sighting. AURORA distinguishes witness accounts, original archived records and interpretations offered by researchers afterward.

В него се описват ярка светлина и твърдения за прекъсвания на комуникационни или приборни системи. За да се тълкуват подобни съобщения, е важно да се проследи коя информация е пряко регистрирана, коя е предадена от свидетели и коя е изложена в служебно резюме.

Един разсекретен документ е силен източник за това как институциите са записали информацията, но не решава самостоятелно всички физически въпроси около събитието. Сравняването на различните участници, времевите интервали и описаните условия е по-полезно от заключение само въз основа на един цитат. Публикуваме оригиналния PDF, за да може читателят да проверява твърденията.

A declassified US document summarizes civilian reports and Iranian military aircraft observations in September 1976. It describes a bright light and reported communication or instrument interruptions. Interpreting such statements requires distinguishing directly recorded information, witness testimony and wording introduced by an official summary.

A declassified document is strong evidence for how institutions recorded the reports, but it cannot alone settle every physical question about the event. Comparing participants, timelines and the reported circumstances is more useful than drawing conclusions from a single passage. The original PDF remains linked so readers can inspect the wording for themselves.

A state mapping camera firing on a timer, and one frame nobody has been able to account for

During a government aerial survey for a hydroelectric project, a cartographic camera firing automatically every 13 seconds recorded a sharp disc-shaped object over Lago de Cote. Nobody on board saw anything; the object was noticed in processing, and it appears on one frame and on neither neighbour.
Source assessment: None. The Instituto Geográfico Nacional made no determination. The negative was retained in state custody.

Reported alternative 1: An emulsion defect or an optical artefact of the lens. Independent examinations report a defined edge and illumination consistent with the sun angle of the rest of the frame, which is not what defects usually look like.
Reported alternative 2: An object on or just above the water, such as a boat or floating debris. The disc overlaps the shoreline, which constrains the geometry but does not settle it.
Reported alternative 3: An insertion made during processing. No analysis has reported evidence of montage, and the negative has stayed with the state since the flight.

summary.en: In the early hours of 24 October 1968 airmen at missile sites around Minot AFB in North Dakota reported a bright light, and a B-52 flying practice approaches near the base had an unidentified return on its own radar. The crew photographed the scope, and while the return stayed with the aircraft its UHF transmitter would not work. Project Blue Book’s record card gives “Possible (PLASMA)” for the radar and for the sighting from the aircraft, and “Probable (AIRCRAFT)(B-52)” and “Probable Astro (SIRIUS)” for the sightings from the ground (NAID 302580672, image 1). The base’s report had listed among “FOUR OCCURANCES THAT CANNOT BE CORRELATED OR EXPLAINED AT THIS LEVEL” “WHAT CAUSED THE AIRCRAFT RADAR ECHO” and the “AIRCRAFT LOSS OF UHF TRANSMISSION” (image 15). The scope photographs are not in the file as published.

A return on a B-52’s radar, photographed on the scope while the bomber’s transmitter failed, and lights seen from missile sites around the base. Blue Book’s card reads “Possible (PLASMA)” for the radar; the base wrote that the echo could not be explained at its level

In the early hours of 24 October 1968 airmen at missile sites around Minot AFB in North Dakota reported a bright light, and a B-52 flying practice approaches near the base had an unidentified return on its own radar. The crew photographed the scope, and while the return stayed with the aircraft its UHF transmitter would not work. Project Blue Book’s record card gives “Possible (PLASMA)” for the radar and for the sighting from the aircraft, and “Probable (AIRCRAFT)(B-52)” and “Probable Astro (SIRIUS)” for the sightings from the ground (NAID 302580672, image 1). The base’s report had listed among “FOUR OCCURANCES THAT CANNOT BE CORRELATED OR EXPLAINED AT THIS LEVEL” “WHAT CAUSED THE AIRCRAFT RADAR ECHO” and the “AIRCRAFT LOSS OF UHF TRANSMISSION” (image 15). The scope photographs are not in the file as published.

Source assessment: Project Blue Book’s record card concludes: for the sightings from the ground, “1. Probable (AIRCRAFT)(B-52) 2. Probable Astro (SIRIUS)”; for the radar, “Possible (PLASMA)”; for the sighting from the aircraft, “Possible (PLASMA)” (NAID 302580672, image 1). Its comment: “The B-52 radar contact and the temporary loss of UHF transmission could be attributed to plasma, similar to ball lighting.” On 1 November 1968, “AFTER REVIEWING PRELIMINARY INFORMATION”, Lt Col Hector Quintanilla of the Foreign Technology Division had wired Strategic Air Command that the UFO painted by the B-52 on radar “IS MOST PROBABLY A PLASMA OF THE BALL-LIGHTNING CLASS” (image 95). The base’s own report of 29 October listed among “FOUR OCCURANCES THAT CANNOT BE CORRELATED OR EXPLAINED AT THIS LEVEL”: “(A) WHAT CAUSED THE AIRCRAFT RADAR ECHO. (B) AIRCRAFT LOSS OF UHF TRANSMISSION.” (image 15)

Reported alternative 1: Plasma of the ball-lightning class, the card’s label for the radar return and the sighting from the aircraft, given as “Possible”. The Foreign Technology Division’s background notes say that “Plasmas can effect electrical equipment and can also be painted on radar” and that “Plasmas, such as ball lightning, can occur in clear weather as well as stormy weather” (image 105). The idea enters the file on 1 November 1968, in a memo on a talk with Mr Goff, TDPA, “who is quite familiar with air-borne radars”, who felt that a plasma “could account for the radar blip, loss of transmission and some of the visual sightings” (image 26).

Reported alternative 2: A fault in the B-52’s radar or radio. On 29 October Quintanilla was “pretty sure it was either caused by an internal radar malfunction that also caused the blip or because of the inversion he might have also picked up an anomalous blip” (image 18). The base’s investigator thought “it couldn’t be a malfunction because they transmitted before and afterwards”, and added: “The aircraft was not checked out afterwards because the transmission was working.” (image 23)

Reported alternative 3: The B-52 itself and the star Sirius, for the sightings from the ground, as the card concludes. The Foreign Technology Division: “It is entirely possible that the initial sighting and the subsequent activities of the object were in fact the B-52 accomplishing upper airwork.” (image 105)

Reported alternative 4: Something the files do not identify. The base left the echo and the loss of transmission unexplained “AT THIS LEVEL” (image 15), and the card gives plasma for them only as “Possible” (image 1).

en: Source-linked case dossier · disclosure.zone (CC BY 4.0). Date and location are taken from this independent catalog; map coordinates, if present, are approximate reference points.
Seven sightings along the Himalaya in an unevaluated CIA report, and a metal disc in a crater it mentions in one sentence

A CIA information report distributed on 11 April 1968 lists seven sightings of bright objects between 19 February and 25 March 1968, over south Ladakh, north-east Nepal, north Sikkim, western Bhutan and the Kaski region of Nepal. The last entry adds, in one sentence, that a huge metallic disc-shaped object was found in a crater at Baltichaur, five miles north-east of Pokhara. The report is marked not finally evaluated, its source is blacked out, and it says nothing more about the object.

Reported alternative 1: A rocket. The entry for Ladakh on 25 March describes a rocket-like object leaving a trail “at a height of 20-25,000 feet”, which “Appeared from Chang La side and was seen moving towards Demochok, i.e. from north to south.” The report does not say whose it could have been.

Reported alternative 2: Something from the direction of Tibet. For Bhutan the report notes that the direction could be “North-east to South-west, that is, from the direction of Tibet”; for Sikkim it prefers the north-east to south-west direction because it matches the Nepal sighting of the same evening; its country line includes China. It says nothing about what the object was.

Reported alternative 3: A crash. The index of 1974 that lists the report tags it “UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECT, AIRCRAFT ADDIDENT” [sic], and the report's last entry describes a blazing object that disintegrated over Kaski and a metallic object found in a crater. No aircraft is named anywhere in the file.

A prospector’s burns, a circle on a rock and radioactive traces, as the RCMP, the RCAF and federal scientists recorded them in 1967–69

Stefan Michalak, an industrial mechanic from Winnipeg, said that on 20 May 1967, while prospecting north of Falcon Beach, he saw two objects come down, that one landed, and that it burned him as it rose when he had touched it. He was treated for burns that night and his doctor recorded “first degree burns to the upper abdominal wall”; an RCMP constable who saw him that afternoon thought the marks on his chest “looked like marks that were caused by rubbing ash onto the skin”. No radioactivity was found on him or his clothes in May. In June Michalak and a partner brought soil, moss, a steel tape and remnants of his shirt from the site they had found; those samples were radioactive, and in July a federal radiation officer found a smear of radium-226 contamination no larger than 100 square inches in a crack of the rock there. In 1969 a scientist of the National Research Council judged it “highly probable” that crushed uranium ore produced all the radioactivity reported. The RCMP closed its file unable to resolve the burns, his illness and the circle on the rock.

Source assessment: The RCMP, 10 August 1967: “On the other hand, there are certain facts that cannot be denied and cannot be accounted for or explained away. These include his illness, headache and loss of weight during a two week period immediately after the alleged sighting; a fluctuation in his blood cell count that occurred at the same time; the burns to his chest, abdomen and clothing as well as the circle on the rock where he alleges the UFO landed. Our investigation has not been able to resolve any of these points mentioned and we have not been able to account for the inconsistent actions of MICHALAK.” S. E. Hunt of the Radiation Protection Division, 13 September 1967: “The origin of this contamination has yet to be determined.” Peter M. Millman of the National Research Council, 4 February 1969: “all the radioactivity observed could well have been produced by finely crushed uranium ore of the type common at certain uranium mines in Canada. Certainly this was what produced the radioactivity in the metallic specimens, and it is highly probable that the same source produced all the other radioactivity reported.”

Reported alternative 1: A hoax, or evidence planted. The files record doubts, not a finding. Cst. Solotki thought the marks on his chest “looked like marks that were caused by rubbing ash onto the skin”. The RCMP listed “a number of discrepancies in MICHALAK’S story that cannot be explained” and called his removal of the evidence from the site “the largest discrepancy”. A telex of Training Command of May 1968, on metal Michalak said he had found at the centre of the circle, says: “SHOULD THIS BE A HOAX SOMEONE IS GOING TO CONSIDERABLE EFFORT TO PERPETRATE SAME”, and R. J. Traill described that metal as sheet silver coated with “crushed pitchblende ore”.

Reported alternative 2: Hallucination. Professor Roy Craig of the University of Colorado, after a search with Michalak, “felt that Mr. Michalak had perhaps been subjected to halucinations, cause or causes of which could possibly be attributed to past experiences” (Bissky’s report). The RCMP found no record of him at three mental hospitals, and his doctor “couldn’t find anything wrong with him mentally” but thought he had “undergone some kind of a severe ordeal”.

Reported alternative 3: An encounter as he described it, with an object of undetermined nature. The RCMP closed its file listing what it could not explain: “his illness, headache and loss of weight”, “a fluctuation in his blood cell count”, “the burns to his chest, abdomen and clothing as well as the circle on the rock where he alleges the UFO landed”.

Millman of the National Research Council, 4 February 1969: “all the radioactivity observed could well have been produced by finely crushed uranium ore of the type common at certain uranium mines in Canada. Certainly this was what produced the radioactivity in the metallic specimens, and it is highly probable that the same source produced all the other radioactivity reported.”

EN · A hoax, or evidence planted. The files record doubts, not a finding. Cst. Solotki thought the marks on his chest “looked like marks that were caused by rubbing ash onto the skin”. The RCMP listed “a number of discrepancies in MICHALAK’S story that cannot be explained” and called his removal of the evidence from the site “the largest discrepancy”. A telex of Training Command of May 1968, on metal Michalak said he had found at the centre of the circle, says: “SHOULD THIS BE A HOAX SOMEONE IS GOING TO CONSIDERABLE EFFORT TO PERPETRATE SAME”, and R. J. Traill described that metal as sheet silver coated with “crushed pitchblende ore”.

EN · Hallucination. Professor Roy Craig of the University of Colorado, after a search with Michalak, “felt that Mr. Michalak had perhaps been subjected to halucinations, cause or causes of which could possibly be attributed to past experiences” (Bissky’s report). The RCMP found no record of him at three mental hospitals, and his doctor “couldn’t find anything wrong with him mentally” but thought he had “undergone some kind of a severe ordeal”.

EN · An encounter as he described it, with an object of undetermined nature. The RCMP closed its file listing what it could not explain: “his illness, headache and loss of weight”, “a fluctuation in his blood cell count”, “the burns to his chest, abdomen and clothing as well as the circle on the rock where he alleges the UFO landed”.

Alleged Minuteman shutdowns during concurrent UAP sightings

According to officer accounts, in March 1967 a series of Minuteman missiles went to a “no-go” state within a short interval, while security personnel simultaneously reported UAP sightings. This is the most frequently cited argument for UAP interest in nuclear weapons.
Source assessment: The USAF pointed to technical causes, including logic-bus transients during maintenance work. No public document links the faults to any sighting.
Reported alternative 1: A logic circuit fault or electromagnetic interference from maintenance work — the technical hypothesis advanced by the USAF.
Reported alternative 2: Two independent events, a technical fault and a sighting, associated after the fact.
Reported alternative 3: A genuine external factor affecting the systems.

summary.en: On April 6, 1966, schoolchildren and teachers near Melbourne reported seeing an unusual object. ABC interviews preserve witness memories, not proof of any particular origin.

source.name: ABC Australia — The Westall UFO Mystery

bg: На 6 април 1966 г. ученици и преподаватели описват необичаен обект над училището в Уестол, край Мелбърн. През 2026 г. Australian Story събира нови интервюта с очевидци. Оригиналните телевизионни кадри от 1966 г. не са открити, затова съвременният филм представя спомени и журналистическо проучване.

Уестол е случай на групови спомени от училищна среда, които продължават да се обсъждат десетилетия след 6 април 1966 г. Разказите за наблюдаван обект са важна част от местната история, но всеки свидетел описва събитията през своя гледна точка. По-късните интервюта помагат да бъдат запазени тези спомени, без автоматично да потвърждават физическите характеристики или произхода на обекта.

Публикациите на ABC представят съвременна журналистическа работа и разговори със свидетели. Това е и причината да ги обозначим като документални материали, а не като оригинални видеокадри от самото наблюдение. Когато гледаш филма или интервютата, различавай реконструкциите, разказите на очевидци и архивните факти. Наличието на видео на страницата на издателя не означава автоматично, че можем законно да го вградим в AURORA.
en: On April 6, 1966, students and teachers described an unusual object above Westall High School near Melbourne. In 2026, Australian Story collected new eyewitness interviews. The original 1966 television footage has not been found, so the modern documentary presents recollections and journalism.

Westall is a case of collective school-community memories still discussed decades after April 6, 1966. The accounts of an observed object form part of local history, but each witness recalls the event from a distinct viewpoint. Later interviews preserve those memories without independently verifying all claimed physical characteristics or the object's origin.

ABC's later reports present journalism and witness interviews, not recovered original footage of the 1966 observation. The dossier therefore distinguishes documentary material from video taken during the reported event. When viewing the interviews, separate reconstructions, recollections and archival facts. A video published on the broadcaster's website is not automatically licensed for embedding on another site.

An 18-year-old hitchhiker and two police officers report five red lights in a row over a field south-west of Exeter, New Hampshire, in the early hours of 3 September 1965. Blue Book first put them down to an air exercise; its own data placed those aircraft over Exeter before 2 a.m., and the record card concludes “UNIDENTIFIED”

In the early hours of 3 September 1965 an 18-year-old hitchhiker on Route 150 south-west of Exeter, New Hampshire, saw “a group of five bright red lights” over a house and a field, watched them “for about 15 minutes” and went to the police station (NAID 302543878, image 97). Patrolman Eugene F. Bertrand Jr. drove him back; in the field “a group of five bright red lights came from behind a group of trees near us”, so close that Bertrand “fell to the ground and started to draw my gun” (image 99). Patrolman David R. Hunt, called by radio, saw the lights “about ½ mile over a field to the South East” at what he estimated as 100 feet (image 98). Neither the hitchhiker nor Bertrand could make out a form, and Bertrand heard “no sound or vibration” (image 99). The Air Force’s investigating officer found no probable cause (image 100), and Blue Book’s record card concludes “UNIDENTIFIED” (image 1).

Source assessment: Blue Book’s first answer, in a letter to Pease AFB stamped 19 October 1965: “It is our belief that aircraft from this operation and various stars and planets were the causes of the various reports on the night of 2 - 3 September from this area.”, the operation being an Eighth Air Force exercise, “Big Blast” (NAID 302543878, image 2). The Eighth Air Force then reported that by 03/0430Z “the operational portion of the mission was complete”, with ten B-47s due at their initial approach fix between 03/0444Z and 03/0535Z (image 6); Blue Book’s summary puts them “in the traffic pattern over Exeter between 0044 and 0135” local time (image 26). On 11 January 1966 Blue Book told the Air Force’s Office of Information that this information “conflicted with the time of the sighting”, and that the officers’ observation after 2 a.m. was “regarded as UNIDENTIFIED” (image 13). On 9 February 1966 the Office of Information wrote: “we have been unable to identify the object you observed on September 3, 1965.” (image 16) The summary: “Since no aircraft can be placed in the area at 0200 hours the case is listed as unidentified by the Air Force.” (image 26) Blue Book’s letter of 3 March 1966 keeps the label “for statistical purposes” and adds: “There is a total lack of evidence to indicate that the sighting could not have been caused by conventional aircraft.” (image 17)

Reported alternative 1: Aircraft of the Eighth Air Force exercise “Big Blast”. The Eighth Air Force reported ten B-47s due at their initial approach fix between 03/0444Z and 03/0535Z, and “The town of Exeter is within the traffic pattern utilized by Air Traffic Control in the recovery of these aircraft at Pease AFB, N.H.” (image 6) Blue Book itself wrote that this “conflicted with the time of the sighting” (image 13): the hitchhiker puts his sighting at 0200 (image 97), and Hunt was called at about 0255 (image 98).

Reported alternative 2: An aircraft with infra-red lights on a photographic mission, or a conventional aircraft with rotating beacons, which Blue Book still held possible on 3 March 1966 (image 17). Pease had answered on 11 February 1966 that crews landing that night made “NO PILOT REPORTS CONCERNING UNUSUAL SIGHTINGS”, and: “ALSO NOT LIKELY THAT AIRCRAFT IS AREA WITH PHOTOGRAPHS OR SPECIAL ELECTRONIC EQUIPMENT DURING THIS TIME.” (image 20)

Reported alternative 3: Something the files do not identify. Blue Book’s summary: “Since no aircraft can be placed in the area at 0200 hours the case is listed as unidentified by the Air Force.” (image 26) The investigating officer at Pease: “At this time have been unable to arrive at a probable cause of this sighting.” (image 100)

summary.en: On 24 April 1964, at about 5:45 p.m., Officer Lonnie Zamora of the Socorro Police Department, New Mexico, broke off a chase to check on a roar and a flame south of the town. In the account he gave that night, an object stood off the road with two people beside it: “TWO PERSONS IN APPARENT WHITE COVERALLS”, as the FBI’s teletype put it the next day (Section 9, p. 226), who “appeared normal in shape--but possibly they were small adults or large kids” (Serial 438, p. 12). The object then rose with a roar and a flame and flew off. The state police sergeant and the undersheriff who answered his radio calls found four smouldering areas and four depressions; that evening Capt. R. T. Holder measured them while an FBI agent set rocks around them. Project Blue Book’s record card marks the case “Unknown” and comments: “Effort to date cannot place vehicle at site. Case carried as UNIDENTIFIED pending additional data.” (NAID 302532129, image 4)

A police officer’s account of an object on the ground and two people beside it, marks in the ground measured at the site the same evening, and a Blue Book card that carries the case “as UNIDENTIFIED pending additional data”

On 24 April 1964, at about 5:45 p.m., Officer Lonnie Zamora of the Socorro Police Department, New Mexico, broke off a chase to check on a roar and a flame south of the town. In the account he gave that night, an object stood off the road with two people beside it: “TWO PERSONS IN APPARENT WHITE COVERALLS”, as the FBI’s teletype put it the next day (Section 9, p. 226), who “appeared normal in shape--but possibly they were small adults or large kids” (Serial 438, p. 12). The object then rose with a roar and a flame and flew off. The state police sergeant and the undersheriff who answered his radio calls found four smouldering areas and four depressions; that evening Capt. R. T. Holder measured them while an FBI agent set rocks around them. Project Blue Book’s record card marks the case “Unknown” and comments: “Effort to date cannot place vehicle at site. Case carried as UNIDENTIFIED pending additional data.” (NAID 302532129, image 4)

Source assessment: Project Blue Book’s record card marks “Unknown” with an “x”, types “UNIDENTIFIED” on the “Other” line and comments: “Initially believed to be observation of Lunar module type cofiguration [sic]. Effort to date cannot place vehicle at site. Case carried as UNIDENTIFIED pending additional data.” (NAID 302532129, image 4) On 28 May 1964 the Foreign Technology Division proposed for release to the press a statement by Capt. Hector Quintanilla, chief of its Aerial Phenomena Branch: “The investigators at Wright-Patterson have not been able to identify or determine what type of vehicle or object Mr Lonnie Zamora observed on 24 April at Socorro, New Mexico.” It ends: “This case is still open and the investigation is still in progress.” (image 15) In April 1965 J. Allen Hynek, whom the Air Force had sent to Socorro, wrote: “Both Quintanilla and I find it impossible to dismiss it as a hoax unless we have some evidence that there was a hoax.” (image 37)

Reported alternative 1: A hoax, as Donald Menzel and Lyle Boyd proposed in a letter of 19 February 1965 that is not in the file. Hynek summed up their idea: the speeding car was “a deliberate decoy”, and hoaxers released “a balloon with a cardboard or aluminum flying saucer attached thereto” (image 46). He answered that “the wind was from the south, and the object went west”, and that no paraphernalia had been found, “such as tubes of helium” (image 46).

Reported alternative 2: A helicopter. The Foreign Technology Division wrote on 28 May 1964: “All military helos including those associated with Project Cloud Gap have been eliminated as a possible cause of the sighting. However, civilian helicopter activity was not completely determined.” (image 14)

Reported alternative 3: A VTOL aircraft. In the same letter: “VTOL type a/c were not eliminated as a possible cause due to the absence of a blast effect in the area.” The people consulted “were not aware of an operational craft of this nature.” (image 15)
Reported alternative 4: A vehicle of “Lunar module type cofiguration [sic]”, which the card says was “Initially believed”; it goes on: “Effort to date cannot place vehicle at site.” (image 4)

A Rio radio report of a metal sphere with a body inside, in a Bahia town that, by the U.S. consul’s account, had seen nothing

On 8 November 1963 Radio Tupi in Rio de Janeiro reported that a large metal sphere with windows had fallen in the centre of Conde, in Bahia, gouging a hole four metres deep, with a human body inside. The Foreign Broadcast Information Service took the report down, and a note on its transcript dated 13 November records a request to the State Department to say whether the embassy had anything more. The embassy in Rio asked its consulate in Salvador. On 20 November it sent the Department an airgram titled “Negative Report on UFO”: the consul wrote that no one in the area had seen such an object and called the story “apparently fabricated in Rio”, and two Salvador papers had carried a denial by the Ministry of Aeronautics and a piece called “The Airship that wasn’t there”. The Department marked the airgram “NOTED - NO ACTION” and filed it.

Source assessment: The consul in Salvador, Harold Midkiff, in his telegram 157 of 14 November 1963 as the embassy quotes it in airgram A-628: “Story of strange object descending in region of Conde Bahia apparently fabricated in Rio no such objects seen by anyone in the area according to newspaper reporters and others who rushed there before investigation reports were received Secretary Public Security speculated object might be weather balloon but no such sighting verified.” The embassy titled the airgram “Negative Report on UFO (Unidentified Flying Object)”. The Department marked it “NOTED - NO ACTION” on 26 November and filed it. The denial by the Ministry of Aeronautics is known only from the airgram’s summary of a newspaper.

Reported alternative 1: A story made up in Rio. The consul in Salvador, in his telegram of 14 November 1963 as the embassy quotes it: “Story of strange object descending in region of Conde Bahia apparently fabricated in Rio”. The documents do not say who made it up or how it reached Radio Tupi.

Reported alternative 2: A weather balloon. The embassy’s telegram of 14 November understood that “an object had been sighted aloft in that vicinity around that date” and that it “had been tentatively identified as weather-type balloon”. In the consul’s reply it is only a speculation: the Secretary of Public Security “speculated object might be weather balloon but no such sighting verified.”

Reported alternative 3: Nothing fell in Conde. The Diario de Noticias of 9 November, as the airgram summarises it, “states that the Ministry of Aeronautics categorically denies that there was any ‘strange object’ in Conde”, and the Jornal da Bahia of 11 November “is entitled ‘The Airship that wasn’t there’”. The embassy had recorded on 14 November that “no repeat no such object had been found aground”.

Reported alternative 4: A real crash. It rests only on the Radio Tupi report, as FBIS took it down, and on a local newspaper report that the embassy paraphrases without naming the paper. No document names a witness, and by the consul’s account the newspaper reporters and others who went to the area found no one who had seen such an object.

A couple driving south on Route 3 near Lincoln, New Hampshire, on the night of 19/20 September 1961 report a lighted object that hovered and seemed to swoop down toward their car. The Air Force took their account by telephone and carries the case as “insufficient data”; the story of an abduction reaches the file only through the press of 1965–66

On the night of 19/20 September 1961, “between 20/0001 and 20/0100”, a couple driving south on Route 3 near Lincoln, New Hampshire, saw “a strange object in the sky” (NAID 28994718, image 39). By the Air Force’s report, taken by telephone, it was a “Continious [sic] band of lights - cigar shaped at all times despite changes of direction”, from which “wings seemed to appear” with red lights on the tips; it stopped and hovered, then seemed “to swoop down in the general direction of their auto”, and as they drove off they heard “a series of short loud ‘buzzes’” (image 40). The record card marks the case “Other”, with “INSUFF DATA” written by hand (our reading), and says the source of the light “is not known” (NAID 28994660, image 1). Four years later the Boston Traveler reported an abduction “related by a New Hampshire couple under clinical hypnosis” (image 30); the file holds that story only in the press.

Source assessment: The record card (NAID 28994660, image 1) marks “Other”, with a typed entry struck out and “INSUFF DATA” written by hand (our reading), and comments: “Both radar and visual sighting are probably due to conditions resulting fm strong inversion which prevaled [sic] in area on morning of sighting. Actual source of light viewed is not known but it has all characteristics of an advertising search light.” The analysis sheet has “OBSERVATION DUE TO UNUSUAL OPTICAL CONDITION RESULTING FROM ATMOSPHERIC CONDITIONS.” (image 2) In 1963 the Air Force’s Foreign Technology Division wrote: “The case is carried as insufficient data in the Air Force Files.”, and, in the same paragraph: “As no lateral or vertical movement was noted, the object was in all probability Jupiter.” (image 4) The report of 1961 describes the object changing direction, hovering and descending toward the car (NAID 28994718, images 40–41). Blue Book’s index evaluates the visual and the radar sighting as “1. Insufficient Data 2. Insufficient Data” (NAID 28921348, image 259).

Reported alternative 1: Jupiter. The Foreign Technology Division’s letter of 27 September 1963: “The planet Jupiter was in the South West, at about 20 degrees elevation and would have set at the approximate time that the object disappeared.” The same letter: “Without positional data the case could not be evaluated as Jupiter.” (NAID 28994660, image 4) Against it, the report of 1961: the object “changed directions rather abruptly and then headed South”, “stopped and hovered in the air”, and in the wife’s account “ascended and descended numerous times very rapidly” (NAID 28994718, images 40–41). APRO’s bulletin of March 1963 has Mrs. Hill describing the object “as bei

Reported alternative 2: An advertising searchlight, the record card’s comment: the light “has all characteristics of an advertising search light” (NAID 28994660, image 1). No document in the file names a searchlight in the area.

Reported alternative 3: An optical effect of a temperature inversion. The analysis sheet: “OBSERVATION DUE TO UNUSUAL OPTICAL CONDITION RESULTING FROM ATMOSPHERIC CONDITIONS.” (image 2) For the analysis the Foreign Technology Division obtained upper-air soundings from Portland, Maine, because “Lincoln, New Hampshire, does not take rawinsonde observations, and Portland, Maine, is the closest station.” (NAID 28994718, image 43; the charts are images 5–53 of NAID 28994660). No paper in the file works out how the inversion would produce what the couple described.

Reported alternative 4: A narrative produced under hypnosis. The file holds the hypnosis story only in the press. Look, which printed parts of the tapes, quotes the psychiatrist, Dr. Benjamin Simon: “Nothing is absolutely proved to me regarding the alleged ‘abduction.’” and “hypnosis is a pathway to the truth as it is felt and understood by the patient.” (Look, 4 October 1966, p. 45; NAID 28994718, image 13)

Lights and figures over a mission on two June nights in 1959, in a missionary’s notes as the US Air Attaché sent them on

On the evening of 26 June 1959 Reverend W. Gill and people of the mission at Boianai watched a bright white light in the north-west, and on it what his data sheet records as “Now three men - moving, glowing, doing something on deck.” That night 38 of them were gathered in one room, three drew what they had seen, and “27 observers of a total of 38 voluntarily signed”. The next evening Gill waved, and “all four now seemed to wave back.” The papers are in a Project Blue Book file: a report of the US Air Attaché in Australia of January 1960, with a civilian society’s report, copies of Gill’s notes and an evaluation by “an interested local agency”, which put at least some of the lights down to the planets Jupiter, Saturn and Mars. The attaché concurred.

Source assessment: The Project Blue Book record card gives the conclusion “Other”: “Misinterpretation of Astro Bodies”. The evaluation in the US Air Attaché’s report of 21 January 1960 finds that “an analysis of rough bearings and angles above the horizon does suggest that at least some of the lights observed were the planets Jupiter, Saturn and Mars”, and the attaché wrote: “This office concurs with the conclusions drawn in paragraph h above.” A letter of 22 February 1960 from Squadron Leader F. A. Lang, which the APRO Bulletin printed as the “RAAF Statement on Gill Sightings”, says that “An officer of this Directorate has investigated” Gill’s report, that “such reports are not releasable to the public”, and that “at least three of the lights were planets, e.g., Jupiter, Saturn and Mars.”

Reported alternative 1: Planets seen through cloud. The evaluation in the attaché’s report: “Although it is not possible to draw firm conclusions, an analysis of rough bearings and angles above the horizon does suggest that at least some of the lights observed were the planets Jupiter, Saturn and Mars. Light refraction, the changing position of the planet relative to the observer and cloud movement would give the impression of size and rapid movement. In addition, varying cloud densities could account for the human shapes and their sudden appearance and disappearance.” The RAAF letter of 22 February 1960 says the same of “at least three of the lights”. Neither gives

Reported alternative 2: Artificial satellites. The record card: “US and USSR satellites were also indicated as possibly being responsible.” The evaluation in the attaché’s report names satellites only for earlier lights: “Probably the constant light and the intermittent light observed in November 1958 were the USSR and US Satellites.” On 26 June Gill himself noted “All UFO’s very clear - satellites?”

Photographs taken from the deck of a Brazilian Navy ship, released by the President

Lights reported around Levelland, Texas, on the night of 2/3 November 1957. Of the six people the Air Force questioned, two said their engines stopped; its field report ends “forwarded as unresolved”, and the record card concludes “Ball lightning”

On the night of 2/3 November 1957 people around Levelland, Texas, reported lights, and some said their vehicles failed. The 1006th Air Intelligence Service Squadron questioned six of them, and its report of 8 November sums up: “Only one observer (Part One) said an object hovered over or on the ground.” Others “saw a light streak across the sky (Parts Three and Four) or a bolt of lightning (Part Five).” (NAID 28972840, image 78) In Part One a student’s engine, lights and radio went out, and when the object left “the motor started with no difficulty” (image 62); in Part Two a barber’s truck engine and lights went out and came back (image 65), an account the reporting officer said “cannot be relied upon” (image 78). The report ends: “this sighting is forwarded as unresolved.” (image 78) The record card concludes “Ball lightning” (image 1).

Source assessment: The record card marks “Other” and writes “Ball lightning”, with the comment: “After very extensive checks and detailed investigations by the Air Force and with complete collaboration with both Air Force & non-governmental scientists it was concluded that the sighting was due to a very rare phenomena, ball lightning.” (NAID 28972840, image 1) Blue Book’s index has “5120 2-3 Levelland, Texas (Folder) (*) Multi Other (BALL LIGHTNING)” (NAID 28921348, image 176). The same files hold doubts about that label. The field report of 8 November: “It is felt that insufficient knowledge of the above phenomena exists at this organization to completely resolve this sighting. Therefore, this sighting is forwarded as unresolved.” (image 78) A comment of 5 December 1957 for ATIC’s analyst: “it is not felt that ball lightning is sufficiently respectable scientifically to be brought into use in explaining any of these sightings, particularly where ordinary lightning appears to furnish an adequate basis for explanations” (image 24). ATIC’s message of 8 November had listed ball lightning among “THE FOLLOWING POSSIBILITIES, REPEAT POSSIBILITIES, BEING CHECKED” (image 34); the analyst’s conclusion of 3 January 1958 begins “In the opinion of the undersigned” (image 23); and a summary says: “No definite conclusion has been reached regarding the possible effects of ball lightning on ignition systems.” (image 36)

Reported alternative 1: Ball lightning or St. Elmo’s fire, the card’s label (image 1). The investigator’s first message gave “ST ELMO FIRE OR THE LIKE” (image 19), and the field report lists “Weather phenomena, such as St. Elmo Fire on a similar phenomenon” and “Bald [sic] lightning. There were Nimbus clouds in the area, which, according to information at this organization must be present for ball lightning to occur.” (image 78) Against it, the comment of 5 December 1957: “it is not felt that ball lightning is sufficiently respectable scientifically to be brought into use in explaining any of these sightings” (image 24).

Reported alternative 2: Ordinary lightning, and water in the ignition. The comment of 5 December 1957: “It appears that ordinary lightning, in one form or another, close at hand, may serve well to explain most of the sightings.” and “It is not unlikely that the ignition of an old car could be put out of order by water (blown or splashed onto it).” (image 24) Of the first sighting it writes: “After Wright got back into the car a flash of lightning close by might have left an after image in his eyes”, and “Thus ordinary lightning and ordinary events might have given rise to the observations of sighting #1.” (image 25) In Part Five a sergeant’s lights and radio went ou

Reported alternative 3: A reflection of burning gas off the low clouds. The investigator’s first message: “POSSIBILITY OF EXCESS BURNING GAS FROMOIL OPERATIONS REFLECTION OFF 400 FOOT CLOUD COVER” (image 19); the field report: “Reflection of excess burning gas from a very low cloud cover.” (image 78, point 2c) Its check with the oil companies found that “a limited amount of excess gas from oil operations was being burned. Most of the gas is returned to the ground.” (image 75)

Reported alternative 4: A cascade of reports after the news. The record card: “This case triggered off more than 300 similarly described reports within a 6 day period because of the nation-wide publicity and sensationalism given by the press, radio and TV.” (image 1) On a report from New Mexico of 6 November someone wrote by hand: “Good example of Mass Suggestion resulting from the Levelland Case” (NAID 28973206, image 2). On the night itself, two of the six sources were out looking for an object that had already been reported (images 68–69).

An unsigned letter, analyses known only from a private bulletin, and an Air Force request for a sample

On 14 September 1957, by the account of the Aerial Phenomena Research Organization (APRO), a private group in Alamogordo, New Mexico, the columnist Ibrahim Sued of the Rio de Janeiro daily “O Globo” printed a reader’s letter: fishing near Ubatuba, the writer had seen a flying disk explode in flames and had picked up fragments “as light as paper”, a sample of which he enclosed. “The signature was not legible.” The only papers on the event in the Project Blue Book files are a Blue Book list that names it among “NOT CASES”, APRO’s bulletins of 1960, which report analyses in Brazil that found magnesium “of a high degree of purity”, and the correspondence of 1960 in which the Air Force asked APRO for a sample. No laboratory report and no analysis by the Air Force is in the files.

Source assessment: Project Blue Book entered the event on its list “1 - 17 SEPTEMBER 1957 SIGHTINGS” under “ADDITIONAL REPORTED SIGHTINGS (NOT CASES)”, as “Early Sep / Ubatuba Beach”, source “APRO Bulletin”, and left the evaluation blank. On 4 May 1960 the Aerospace Technical Intelligence Center suggested that APRO “be requested to forward a sample of the material and the technical report concerning the Ubatuba Beach case to ATIC”, and added: “For your information, the details of the Ubatuba Beach sighting closely parallel the circumstances of a case which took place near Maury Island, Washington 21 June 1947. … The Air Force conclusion is that the Maury Island case was probably a hoax.” No analysis by the Air Force is in the files.

Reported alternative 1: A hoax, by comparison. ATIC’s memo of 4 May 1960 sets the story beside the Maury Island case of 1947, of which “The Air Force conclusion is that the Maury Island case was probably a hoax.” The memo does not call the Ubatuba case a hoax.

Reported alternative 2: Fragments of a flying disc, as APRO concluded: “On the basis of this study, it is highly probable that the metallic chunks picked up on a beach near Ubatuba, Sao Paulo, are really fragments of a flying disc.” The analyses it rests on are known only from APRO’s account.

A signal on an electronic reconnaissance aircraft’s direction finder and a light seen from its cockpit. Blue Book’s card reads “Was Aircraft”; the Air Technical Intelligence Center found it “impossible to make any determination”

Early on 17 July 1957 an RB-47H electronic reconnaissance aircraft of the 55th Strategic Reconnaissance Wing, callsign Lacy 17, was flying over the southern United States. Near Meridian, Mississippi, its ECM operator No. 2 picked up a signal of “2995 MC TO 3000 MC” that moved up his direction-finding scope, which the wing read as “AN AIRBORNE SOURCE”. From 1010Z the aircraft commander and co-pilot saw a bright light; for the next 90 minutes, as far as Oklahoma City, the wing’s message follows the signal’s bearings and the crew’s sightings, and its intelligence officer had “NO DOUBT” that they coincided. By the same message the air defence site “Utah” confirmed the object on its scopes; the same day the radar squadron at Duncanville, Texas, wrote of “NEGATIVE CONTACT WITH OBJECT”, and the commander called the attempt to find it on the aircraft’s own radar “UNSUCCESSFUL”. Project Blue Book’s record card concludes “Was Aircraft”, with the comment “Identified as american Airlines flight 655.” (NAID 28970538, image 1). The Air Technical Intelligence Center had written: “it is impossible to make any determination from the information submitted. On the other hand, it is difficult to conclude that nothing was present, in the face of the visual and other data presented.” (image 7)

Source assessment: Project Blue Book’s record card concludes “Was Aircraft”, with the comment “Identified as american Airlines flight 655.” (NAID 28970538, image 1). Beside it a handwritten note, by an unknown hand and of unknown date, reads “Hogwash”. An undated handwritten summary in the file gives the reason: “it was definitely established by the CAA that object observed in the vicinity of Dallas and Ft. Worth was an airliner” (image 13). The Civil Aeronautics Administration’s letter in the file, of 8 November 1957, concerns an incident “near El Paso, Texas” that “involved American Airlines’ Flight No. 655”, in which “the unidentified flying object was American Airlines’ Flight No. 966” (image 9); it does not mention the RB-47, Dallas or Fort Worth (our reading). Earlier, on 30 October 1957, the Air Technical Intelligence Center’s AFCIN-4E1 had written: “it is impossible to make any determination from the information submitted. On the other hand, it is difficult to conclude that nothing was present, in the face of the visual and other data presented.” (image 7) On 17 October 1957 the Air Defense Command wrote: “This Command is unable to offer any explanation for the sighting. Therefore, this sighting is being carried as unknown.” (image 11)

Reported alternative 1: Ground radars received on the direction finder. AFCIN-4E1 wrote in 1957 that the signals “have all the characteristics of ground radar equipment, and in fact are similar to CPS-6B. This office knows of no S-band airborne equipment having the characteristics outlined.” (image 7) In 1971 Philip J. Klass argued that they came from such radars “near Biloxi and Duncanville”, the first one shown 180 degrees off, and moving up the scope, by a possible fault in the receiver (images 21–38).

Reported alternative 2: An airliner, as the card says. The letter on which its identification seems to rest concerns a sighting near El Paso (image 9, our reading). Klass suggested that American Airlines flight 966, approaching Dallas, may have been the target the Duncanville radar saw between 10:48Z and 10:56Z, but wrote that “this particular airliner could not have been the ‘visible UFO’ seen by the RB-47 crew at 10:39Z” (image 34).
Reported alternative 3: A meteor for the first light: the light that “flashed by the RB-47 at 10:10Z”, Klass wrote, “had all the earmarks of a bright meteor” (image 36).

Reported alternative 4: An airborne source of the signal, as the wing’s intelligence officer concluded in 1957: “55SRW DOI HAS NO DOUBT THE ELECTRONIC D/F’S COINCIDED EXACTLY WITH VISUAL OBSERVATIONS BY A/C NUMEROUS TIMES THUS INDICATING POSITIVELY THE OBJECT BEING THE SIGNAL SOURCE.” (image 44)

Radar targets and lights over RAF Bentwaters and RAF Lakenheath, and an RAF Venom sent after one of them. Blue Book’s card reads “Anam. [sic] Propagation”; the same file calls its information incomplete

On the evening of 13 August 1956 the GCA radar at RAF Bentwaters in England tracked targets that its operators put at up to “more than 4,000 miles per hour”. After midnight the radar centre at RAF Lakenheath tracked targets, ground observers there reported white lights, and an RAF Venom sent after one target reported it on its own radar; Lakenheath’s controllers reported that the target then began “A TAIL CHASE OF THE FRIENDLY FIGHTER”. Project Blue Book’s record card concludes “Anam. [sic] Propagation” (NAID 28966873, image 1), “On the basis of the above, and the limited data provided” (image 3). The same file says the radar and visual sightings “cannot be considered as concurrent” (image 1) and that “From the incomplete information submitted, it is impossible to make a definite determination of the sources of these sightings” (image 33).

Source assessment: Project Blue Book’s record card enters its conclusion on the “Other” line: “Anam. [sic] Propagation” (NAID 28966873, image 1). The comment beneath it reaches it “On the basis of the above, and the limited data provided”: “there is no compelling reason to conclude that the radar UFO sightings were other than the result of anomalous propagation” (image 3). It also says that the radar, ground and air observations “cannot be considered as concurrent” (image 1). An analysis of 31 August 1956 in the same file: “From the incomplete information submitted, it is impossible to make a definite determination of the sources of these sightings”; among the missing data it names “scope photographs, weather information indicating presence or lack of temperature inversion, moisture lapse data” (image 33). On the meteors put forward for the visual sightings, the Air Force’s consultant J. Allen Hynek wrote on 17 October 1956: “It seems highly unlikely, for instance, that the Perseid meteors could have been the cause of the sightings” (image 27).

en: Source-linked case dossier · disclosure.zone (CC BY 4.0). Date and location are taken from this independent catalog; map coordinates, if present, are approximate reference points.
Four Americans in one train, four different objects, and an agency that took down every account before it gave a verdict

In October 1955 four Americans on a train from Baku to Tiflis saw lights rise from an airfield between the line and the Caspian Sea. Within six weeks the CIA had written three documents about it: a memorandum after interviewing one of them, a memorandum after interviewing all four, and an unevaluated information report from one of the party. The four described four different things. The CIA found that only one account supported an unconventional aircraft, that the rest could probably be explained as steep-climbing aircraft or missiles, and that the evidence was not firm enough to conclude the Soviets had a radically new type of aircraft.

Source assessment: The CIA's Assistant Director for Scientific Intelligence reported to the Director of Central Intelligence on 31 October 1955, after all four participants had been debriefed: "the only testimony which would support the existence of flying saucers or radically unconventional aircraft is that of Colonel Hathaway. All other observations can probably be explained as steep climbing aircraft or missiles." He added that further discussions would probably be required, and that "the evidence does not appear sufficiently firm to warrant the conclusion that the Soviets have developed and have in operation a radically new type of aircraft."

Reported alternative 1: Steep-climbing aircraft or missiles from the airfield. The CIA's reading of three of the four accounts, qualified as "probably". It sits with the searchlight on the field and the launch the information report describes, and it leaves Colonel Hathaway's account unexplained.
Reported alternative 2: A radically new Soviet aircraft. The question the CIA was asking. It found the evidence not firm enough; only Colonel Hathaway's account supports it.

Reported alternative 3: More than one object. The memorandum of 31 October says the others saw "another object" a few minutes after the senator's, and the information report records "the second launching in rapid succession". The four accounts need not describe the same thing.

en: Source-linked case dossier · disclosure.zone (CC BY 4.0). Date and location are taken from this independent catalog; map coordinates, if present, are approximate reference points.
A night at a farmhouse near Kelly, Kentucky, in a newspaper, a witness statement and the Air Force’s later papers

On the night of 21 August 1955 two cars full of people from a farmhouse near Kelly drove to the police station in Hopkinsville and said that little men from a space ship had attacked the house: “We’ve been fighting them for nearly four hours”. They had fired at them with “a shotgun for Sutton and a .22 caliber target pistol for Taylor”. More than a dozen officers went out and found “no tracks of ‘little men’” and no mark of a landing, only a hole in a window screen where the occupants said they had fired. The papers in the US releases are in a Project Blue Book file: a copy of the local paper of 22 August, a statement written that day, a United Press dispatch, and the Air Force’s inquiries of 1956–57. No official investigation is on record; in 1957 the Air Force’s intelligence center wrote that “no credence can be given this almost fantastic report”.

Source assessment: No report of an official investigation is in the file. The Air Technical Intelligence Center to Campbell Air Force Base, 29 August 1957: “Lacking factual, confirming data, no credence can be given this almost fantastic report. As the incident has never been officially reported to the Air Force, it has not taken official cognizance of the matter.” Campbell AFB replied that the Sheriff’s Office and the Hopkinsville police had been asked and “Neither had a report of investigation on file”. A statement taken at the base on 26 September 1957 ends: “It is felt that the report cannot be substantiated as far as any actual object appearing in the vicinity at that time.” The separator sheet in the Blue Book file is marked “No Case”.

Reported alternative 1: A monkey escaped from a circus. Major John E. Albert, who went to the farm on 22 August 1955, gave it as his opinion in 1957 that “at the time, there was a circus in the area and a monkey might have escaped, giving the appearance of a small man.” An undated paragraph written after September 1956 records a report of “a circus train near town a day or two before. However, this cannot be confirmed”, and that in the opinion of Dr. Hynek and its author, “if so, it is possible that some monkeys or apes escaped during the night.”

Reported alternative 2: Imaginations worked up after a religious meeting and a picture. Albert, in the same statement: the woman and her family had been at a religious meeting and had discussed an article with “a picture which appeared to be a little man when it actually was a monkey, painted silver”, so that “their imaginations ran away with them and they really did believe what they saw, which they thought was a little man.”

Reported alternative 3: An encounter with something of undetermined nature. The household told the police, the press and later interviewers of figures that bullets did not stop; nothing the officers found that night confirms or rules it out.

A tanker crew, a ground radar and an Air Force committee that could not explain the two together

On 6 July 1955 the crew of a USAF KC-97 tanker reported an unidentified airborne object in the Newfoundland area, and a ground radar in the same area obtained a return on an object that apparently was the one the crew were watching. A Headquarters USAF intelligence committee could not explain the simultaneous radar returns and visual sightings, tentatively accepted Northeast Air Command's evaluation of an electrical phenomenon and misinterpretation by the crew, classified the incident as an unidentified flying object, and recommended that fighters be scrambled without delay in future incidents of this kind. The crew's accounts, the radar data and the original messages are not in the released file.

Source assessment: Headquarters USAF committee, as sent to the Royal Canadian Air Force in August 1955: “The committee was unable to explain the simultaneous ground radar returns and aircrew visual sightings, and tentatively attributes the incident to electrical phenomenon and misinterpretation of the sightings by aircrew members.” And: “That this incident be classified as an Unidentified Flying Object.”

Reported alternative 1: An electrical phenomenon and misinterpretation by the aircrew. Northeast Air Command's evaluation, which the Headquarters USAF committee accepted tentatively while saying it could not explain the simultaneous radar returns and visual sightings. The file does not say what electrical phenomenon was meant.

Reported alternative 2: A high performance unconventional aircraft. The committee “discussed the possibility that the object might have been an high performance unconventional aircraft”, and found that “no intelligence is available to support or deny the existence of unconventional Soviet aircraft comparable to those under consideration in the US and Canada and providing performance such as reported.” The file names no aircraft.

A Headquarters USAF intelligence committee could not explain the simultaneous radar returns and visual sightings, tentatively accepted Northeast Air Command's evaluation of an electrical phenomenon and misinterpretation by the crew, classified the incident as an unidentified flying object, and recommended that fighters be scrambled without delay in future incidents of this kind. The crew's accounts, the radar data and the original messages are not in the released file.

EN · Headquarters USAF committee, as sent to the Royal Canadian Air Force in August 1955: “The committee was unable to explain the simultaneous ground radar returns and aircrew visual sightings, and tentatively attributes the incident to electrical phenomenon and misinterpretation of the sightings by aircrew members.” And: “That this incident be classified as an Unidentified Flying Object.”

EN · An electrical phenomenon and misinterpretation by the aircrew. Northeast Air Command's evaluation, which the Headquarters USAF committee accepted tentatively while saying it could not explain the simultaneous radar returns and visual sightings. The file does not say what electrical phenomenon was meant.

EN · A high performance unconventional aircraft. The committee “discussed the possibility that the object might have been an high performance unconventional aircraft”, and found that “no intelligence is available to support or deny the existence of unconventional Soviet aircraft comparable to those under consideration in the US and Canada and providing performance such as reported.” The file names no aircraft.

Разгледай оригиналните документи и свидетелства чрез връзките по-долу; там са събрани детайлите, снимките и видеоматериалите, когато са публикувани.

Съобщенията от юли 1952 г. включват необичайни радарни отражения и наблюдавани светлини във въздушното пространство около Вашингтон. Тъй като в случая участват както диспечери, така и пилоти, историческата документация е по-сложна от единичен разказ на очевидец. Това не означава, че всички съобщения непременно описват един и същ обект или имат обща причина.

Когато се сравняват радарни и визуални сигнали, трябва да се проверят точните часове, позициите на наблюдателите и обстановката за всеки отделен запис. Архивните файлове на Project Blue Book са подходящо начало за такава проверка. Тук не превръщаме наличието на институционално разследване в доказателство за определена хипотеза.
en: Air traffic controllers and pilots reported unusual radar returns and lights over Washington during July 1952. Historical documents are held in Project Blue Book.
Explore the original documents and testimony through the links below, including recordings and images where the publisher has released them.

The July 1952 reports involved unusual radar returns and observed lights around Washington airspace. Because controllers and pilots were among the people involved, the historical paper trail is more complex than a single eyewitness account. That does not mean every reported return or light represented the same object or shared a cause.

Comparing radar and visual observations requires attention to exact timing, observer location and the conditions of each report. Project Blue Book files provide a historical starting point for this work. The existence of an official investigation is not treated as proof of any particular proposed explanation.

A Navy Chief Photographer, a commissioned warrant officer, and footage the Air Force answered three different ways

A Navy warrant officer and professional aerial photographer shot colour film showing a group of bright objects in motion. The material received one of the most detailed analyses in Blue Book history, including densitometric measurement.

Source assessment: The file holds three answers in sequence, not one. The ATIC worksheet for the sighting, in 1952, marks the final evaluation “Unknown”. A teleconference message from Blue Book of 3 February 1953, supplying text for a press release, calls sea gulls soaring in thermal air currents a “strong possibility” and says the Air Force contemplates no further action. A memorandum prepared for the Air Force press room on 1 June 1956 finds “little reasonable doubt” that the objects were “indeed seagulls”, and credits a seagull conclusion to the Air Force Photo Reconnaissance Laboratory. The laboratory analysis in the same file says the opposite: it is reasonably certain that the brightness of the images exceeds that of any natural diffuse reflector such as white birds against the sky.

Reported alternative 1: Gulls soaring in a thermal. Proposed on the ATIC worksheet in 1952, alongside migrating snow geese, and adopted by the Air Force for the press in 1956. It fits the milling motion and the absence of visible structure, and it runs into the Air Force laboratory’s own finding that the images are brighter than any bird. The CIA’s scientific panel, in January 1953, found the motions, sizes and brightnesses “strongly to suggest birds”, while noting that no data was available on the albedo of birds. The Blue Book file contains neither the frames with identifiable gulls nor the gull test films the 1956 memorandum relies on.

Reported alternative 2: Pillow balloons, December 1952. Officers of the Office of Naval Research and balloon specialists at General Mills in Minneapolis, shown the film eight times, agreed the objects closely resembled pillow balloons in flight; General Mills’ own head of balloon research was the least convinced, finding them a bit too bright and too quick. The Blue Book photo file’s catalogue card gives “Pillow balloons” or birds as the probable explanation. Attempts to trace a launch near Tremonton were negative, and the ATIC worksheet notes there were too many objects for balloons.

Reported alternative 3: Genuine unidentified objects. The Air Force laboratory, without densitometry, judged the images brighter than any bird and the objects non-spherical if they were reflecting light at all. The Navy Photographic Interpretation Center, with densitometry, went further and called them light sources. Its brightness measurements were made on a duplicate of a copy and were rejected by two astronomers as methodologically wrong, its speeds rest on assumptions the report itself calls arbitrary, and the CIA’s scientific panel could not accept its conclusions.

Reported alternative 4: A mirage. Listed first on the ATIC worksheet: no inversion layer, but a very high lapse rate between 4,000 and 10,000 feet. The 1956 Douglas Aircraft analysis considered it and found it hard to square with the clear air and the steady, unshimmering images.
