Formations of lights over Lubbock, Texas, from 25 August 1951, timed by professors of Texas Technical College; photographs by a student that the Air Force’s photographic laboratory could neither confirm nor deny as a record of unknown objects; and an index entry that files the case as “Other (BIRDS)”

From the evening of 25 August 1951 professors of Texas Technical College watched formations of lights pass over Lubbock, Texas: “a series of lights in an arcuate formation which covered about 10° in the sky”, in their own report (NAID 28939743, image 84), or “a ‘V’ or ‘U’ shaped set of light-like objects”, in a later summary (image 19). They timed the flights at thirty degrees per second and saw “ten or twevle [sic] flights” up to about 1 November 1951 (image 85). A college freshman photographed formations of lights at the end of August; the papers give the night as both 30 and 31 August. The Air Force’s photographic laboratory wrote: “It is not possible at this time to confirm or deny the authenticity of these negatives as a record of unknown objects against either a starlit or overcast sky.” (image 90) Blue Book’s index files the case as “Other (BIRDS)” (NAID 28921348, image 42).

Source assessment: Blue Book’s index files the case as “978 25 Lubbock, Texas (FOLDER)* Multiple (PHOTO) Other (BIRDS)”, with the footnote “* IN SEPARATE FOLDER” (NAID 28921348, image 42); the unit holds no record card for the case. An undated summary, which mentions a contact of 1959 and so was written after it (our reading), gives the reasoning: “The Air Force conclusion is that birds, with street lights reflecting from them, were the probable cause of this sighting.” (NAID 28939743, image 19) The papers of 1951 and 1952 leave the question open. A status report: “The possible conclusion is that some people did see birds, but others saw some other objects.” (image 10) A faculty group that watched on 5 September argued that “There would not be enough light from reflections to obtain photographs of a bird in flight at night”, and ATIC commented: “Substantiated by the Photo Section of WADC.” (image 24) The professors told Lt. E. J. Ruppelt: “Birds could not do that.” (image 81) The photographic laboratory could neither confirm nor deny the negatives as a record of unknown objects (image 90). A summary of November 1951 says “no conclusions have yet been reached” (image 111), and Ruppelt said in 1952: “So we're up against a blank wall on this certain, this one case.” (DOW-UAP-D154, p. 9)

Reported alternative 1: Birds lit by the city’s street lights, the label’s explanation. For it: the undated summary, which settles on ducks rather than plovers: “Since plovers do not usually fly in formations of more than six or seven, ducks become the more probable.” (image 19); a man at Brownfield who watched a formation circle his house, “he could see the objects and they were birds”, and who “identified the sound as the call of a plover” (image 74); and a photographer of the Lubbock Avalanche, who saw a flock “visible in the light of the sodium vapor street lights used in Lubbock” (image 71). Against it: the professors, “Birds could not do that.” (image 81); WAD

Reported alternative 2: A mirage of distant lights in a layer of warm air over cold, the hypothesis of the astronomer Donald H. Menzel in LOOK of 17 June 1952 (T5), clipped into the FBI’s file. He imitated the layers with two liquids in a jar: “Finally, when I replaced the single pinhole with a row that simulated distant street lights, the resulting images behaved and looked like the Lubbock Lights.” And: “As I have said earlier, these experiments are suggestive rather than definitive.” (FBI file 62-HQ-83894, Section 6, p. 259)

Reported alternative 3: Faked photographs. The laboratory could not “confirm or deny the authenticity of these negatives as a record of unknown objects” (image 90). Ruppelt, in 1952: “He could have taken a black sheet of paper and just punched holes in it and faked them very easily”, and “We've never been able to prove that they were faked.” (DOW-UAP-D154, p. 8) This would touch the photographs only; the professors said the photographs did not show what they had seen (image 9).

Reported alternative 4: Birds for some sightings and something else for others. A status report: “The possible conclusion is that some people did see birds, but others saw some other objects.” And: “If the photos are authentic, the objects very probably are not ducks” (image 10).

The two most famous UFO photographs ever taken, and the limits of photographic analysis

A farming couple took two photographs of a metallic disc-shaped object. The images passed through several independent analyses, including within the Condon Committee, and to this day have no resolution that all researchers accept.
Source assessment: The Condon Committee judged the photometric analysis consistent with a large distant object, but did not rule out a hoax.
Reported alternative 1: A model suspended on a line beneath the power cable visible in frame — the hypothesis repeatedly advanced in sceptical analyses.
Reported alternative 2: A genuine large object at roughly a kilometre — consistent with part of the photometric work.

An amateur radar, an Air Force radar and a light over the turnpike near a nuclear plant; every check came back empty or a star

Between March 1950 and January 1951 the FBI's file on flying discs collected a run of reports of objects over the Atomic Energy Commission's plant at Oak Ridge, Tennessee. A radio amateur in Knoxville reported an object “directly over Oak Ridge” at up to 100,000 feet on a surplus radar set; the Navy's radar saw nothing, and the Air Force officers who examined his set found it unreliable. In October an Air Force radar at Knoxville tracked eleven objects across the controlled area that a fighter could not find. On 18 December two carloads of officers and engineers saw a bright light over the turnpike, which the three who signed one of the statements compared to sunlight reflected from a distant aircraft. In January 1951 a pilot and the plant's patrol identified a light over the area as a star. The file records every check; none of them found an object, and several of the records it refers to are not in the release.

Reported alternative 1: A faulty set and an unreliable operator, for the March reports. Captain Cross “had very grave doubts as to the capabilities of the surplus APN-7 radar set which had been adapted by ADCOCK”, Colonel Gasser and Captain Cross judged the equipment “haphazard at best”, and the Army reported on 9 March that the “radar set has been modified so as to cast doubt on reliability of reading” (Section 5, pp. 88, 94).

Reported alternative 2: Sunlight reflected from a distant aircraft, for 18 December 1950. The three officers who signed one of the statements wrote: “The object appeared only as the bright reflection of the sun from an apparently metal surface, much as might be expected from an aircraft at a great distance” (Section 6, p. 103).

Reported alternative 3: A star, for 16 January 1951. The pilot sent to look “sighted subject object and reported it to be a star”, and the plant's patrol headquarters reported that the object was “determined (to be a star)” (Section 6, p. 108).

Reported alternative 4: Radar jamming by ionization of particles in the atmosphere. In December 1950 the FBI Director ordered Knoxville to “OBTAIN ALL FACTS CONCERNING POSSIBLE RADAR JAMMING BY IONIZATION OF PARTICLES IN ATMOSPHERE” (Section 6, p. 93). It is a question to be checked, not an answer; the result is not in the release.

A wave over New Mexico’s nuclear installations, and Project Twinkle

A series of vivid green fireballs observed over the most sensitive nuclear installations in the United States. The phenomenon was taken seriously enough that a dedicated observation programme, Project Twinkle, was established with cameras and theodolites.
Source assessment: Project Twinkle ended without resolution. The prevailing hypothesis was unusual bolide activity.
Reported alternative 1: Bolides with high copper content, producing the characteristic green — a hypothesis its own proponent rejected on trajectory grounds.
Reported alternative 2: Electrical phenomena in the upper atmosphere.
Reported alternative 3: An observer-concentration effect: nuclear installations had round-the-clock guards looking at the sky, so they recorded what nobody elsewhere was watching for.

Twenty-five minutes of manoeuvring against a light over Fargo
Second Lieutenant George Gorman flew an extended series of manoeuvres against a small bright light which, by his account, responded to his movements and out-turned him.
Source assessment: Blue Book attributed the event to a lighted weather balloon.
Reported alternative 1: A lighted weather balloon — a drifting object combined with the observer’s own manoeuvres produces the illusion of “response” and “pursuit”.
Reported alternative 2: The planet Jupiter with misjudged distance.

A DC-3 crew’s near-miss over Alabama

Two Eastern Air Lines pilots reported passing a large cigar-shaped object with two rows of bright windows and a flame at the rear. The case was one of the pillars of the internal Project SIGN document said to have argued an interplanetary hypothesis.
Source assessment: Blue Book ultimately classified the event as a bolide (meteor).
Reported alternative 1: A bright bolide breaking up in the atmosphere — the “windows” being fragments seen for a fraction of a second.
Reported alternative 2: A genuine cigar-shaped craft — with no instrumental corroboration of any kind.

On 7 January 1948 the control tower at Godman Field, Kentucky, watched a white object for over an hour and a half, and Capt. Thomas F. Mantell, leading a flight of National Guard P-51s, climbed after it and crashed. Over the years the Air Force’s papers called it Venus, “unexplained” and a balloon, and none ties the balloon to a record of one

Paul I. Orner it “partially appeared as a parachute does with bright sun shining on the top of the silk” (NAID 28930550, image 43); to PFC Stanley Oliver it “had the resemblance of an ice cream cone topped with red” (image 36). The tower asked a flight of four National Guard P-51s passing overhead to try to identify it, and three climbed toward it. By the statement of T/Sgt Quinton A. Blackwell, the flight leader reported it “ahead and above, I'm still climbing” and then: “It appears metallic object of tremendous size” (image 38). The leader was Capt. Thomas F. Mantell (image 40). The last contact was at about 15:15 (image 38), and Mantell’s P-51 “crashed 5 miles SW Franklin, Kentucky” (image 31). The record card has “BALLOON” written by hand (image 1).

Source assessment: The papers give several answers. An astronomer, not named, “attempted to account for this phenomena as either Venus or a comet. (?)”, with no reasons recorded (NAID 28930550, image 11). On 10 November 1948, after the Equipment Laboratory had judged that Venus would probably not be seen so near the Sun (image 18), A. B. Deyarmond of the Intelligence Department wrote: “It is apparent, from the data given above, that the object sighted at Godman Air Force Base on 7 January 1948 was not the planet Venus. Therefore, this sighting must be considered as unexplained.” (image 26) On 5 January 1949 the Air Materiel Command sent the summaries of incidents 1 to 172 to the Air Weather Service “for study and recommendations as to which of the incidents may be eliminated as balloons released on routine synoptic ascents”, and listed incident 33 among those that in its opinion were “having the greatest possibility of being balloons”, adding: “This list does not eliminate the possibility that many of the remaining incidents are balloons.” (NAID 28930193, image 5) Hynek’s evaluations for Project Grudge, undated in the file, list it as astronomical, of “High probability” (NAID 28929152, image 8); an unsigned evaluation of a sighting over Columbus that day, which we read as his, finds that the evidence “fits the hypothesis that the object observed was the planet Venus, and, considered with incidents #30, 33, and 48, it is incredible that it could have been anything else” (NAID 28930193, image 2). The record card has “BALLOON” written by hand, with no date, signature or reason (image 1), and Blue Book’s index has “Balloon” (NAID 28921348, image 15). Capt. Edward J. The Air Materiel Command’s letter of 5 January 1949 put the incident among those “having the greatest possibility of being balloons” and added that its list “does not eliminate the possibility that many of the remaining incidents are balloons” (NAID 28930193, image 5); the record card has “BALLOON” (image 1); and the memorandum of 1956 argued for a “Sky Hook” balloon from its size (DOW-UAP-D102, p. 65). Between 16:30 and 16:45 Central time Dr. Seyfert, an astronomer at Vanderbilt University, saw what he reported as “a pear shaped balloon with cables and a basket attached, moving first SSE, then W, at a speed of 10 miles per hour at

Reported alternative 2: Venus. An astronomer, not named, offered “either Venus or a comet” (image 11), and a note on the check-list for Capt. Carter’s account says: “Does not seem to tally with report that the phenomena was ‘Venus or a comet’” (image 9). summary.bg: През юли 1947 г. се появяват съобщения за намерени останки край Розуел. По-късни американски държавни разследвания свързват материалите с балонна програма, а твърденията за извънземен кораб не са потвърдени.
summary.en: Reports of recovered debris near Roswell emerged in July 1947. Later US government investigations linked the material to balloon research, and claims of an alien craft were not substantiated.

bg: Историята започва с намерени останки край Розуел през юли 1947 г. В следващите десетилетия тя става център на обществени спорове, книги и филми. Докладите на американските ВВС свързват откритите материали с височинна балонна програма, което е важно за историческата документация.

През юли 1947 г. сведенията за намерени отломки край Розуел стават част от ранната история на публичните разкази за летящи чинии. По-късно случаят придобива множество версии, често с взаимно противоречащи си твърдения. За изследователски архив е съществено да се отделят публикациите и документите, близки по време до събитието, от разказите, появили се години по-късно.

Официални американски проверки свързват материалите с балонни изследователски програми, като не установяват доказателства за извънземен апарат. В досието този извод е представен като оценката на цитирания източник, а не като основание да се заличават историческите свидетелства. Полезният въпрос е кои твърдения са подкрепени от документи и кои принадлежат на по-късния фолклор около случая.
en: The story began with recovered debris near Roswell in July 1947. Over subsequent decades it became the subject of books, films and public debate. U.S. Air Force investigations linked the recovered material to a high-altitude balloon program, an important part of the historical record.

Reports about debris recovered near Roswell in July 1947 became part of the early public history of flying saucers. In later decades the incident accumulated many versions, often featuring conflicting claims. A research archive should separate contemporary publications and documents from accounts first circulated years after the event.

Subsequent US government investigations linked the material to balloon research programs and found no substantiation for an alien vehicle. The dossier attributes that conclusion to the cited source without erasing the historical importance of witness accounts. A productive approach is to ask which specific claims are documentary and which belong to later reinterpretation and folklore.

Разгледай оригиналните документи и свидетелства чрез връзките по-долу; там са събрани детайлите, снимките и видеоматериалите, когато са публикувани.

Пилотът Кенет Арнолд съобщава за група бързо движещи се обекти край планината Рейниър на 24 юни 1947 г. Разказът има особено място в публичната история, защото е сред наблюденията, привлекли мащабно медийно внимание към темата за летящите чинии. В тази историческа значимост не бива да се смесват популярността на публикацията и независимата проверка на физическите характеристики на обектите.

За да се реконструира наблюдението, трябва да се разграничат оригиналните формулировки на пилота, интерпретациите в пресата и изчисленията, направени въз основа на субективно оценени дистанции. Архивите на Project Blue Book помагат да се разбере как подобни съобщения са били документирани и разглеждани от американските институции през следващите години.
en: On June 24, 1947, pilot Kenneth Arnold described fast-moving objects near Mount Rainier. Early records preserve one of the accounts that brought widespread attention to flying saucers.
Explore the original documents and testimony through the links below, including recordings and images where the publisher has released them.

Pilot Kenneth Arnold reported fast-moving objects near Mount Rainier on June 24, 1947. The account occupies an important place in public history because it helped bring widespread media attention to flying-saucer reports. That historical significance should not be confused with independent confirmation of the reported objects' physical properties.

Reconstructing the observation requires separating Arnold's original statements, press interpretations and speed estimates based on uncertain perceived distances. Project Blue Book collections provide historical context for how such reports were later documented and assessed by US institutions. The dossier preserves the account without presenting a disputed estimate as a measured fact.

Gravel-pit rock passed off as flying-disc fragments, two Army officers killed hours after being handed a box of it, no sabotage

In August 1947 the FBI and the Fourth Air Force looked into a story that Harold A. Dahl had seen flying discs near Maury Island, in Puget Sound, and that one of them had showered his boat with debris. The story reached the file second-hand, first in a publisher’s letter of 22 July, and its versions disagree on the date, the number of objects and who was aboard. Two Army Air Forces intelligence officers who heard it in a Tacoma hotel on 31 July, and were handed a box of the supposed fragments, were killed hours later when their B-25 crashed near Kelso; the Army and the FBI found no sabotage. On 7 August Dahl and Fred L. Crisman signed a statement for the FBI calling the material “strange rock formations from a gravel pit on Maury Island”, and an Army Air Forces officer compared it with slag at a smelter. No one who said they had seen the discs ever signed an account of them.

Source assessment: The Fourth Air Force A-2 report of 12 August 1947, approved by Lt. Col. Donald L. Springer, recommends “That no further investigation be undertaken on this specific incident by Army Air Force personnel” and that consideration be given to revoking Crisman’s Air Reserve commission “as an undesirable and unreliable officer”; the report still gives the status of the case as “Pending”. For the FBI, D. M. Ladd reported to the Director on 14 August 1947: “Investigation by the Bureau has reflected that this plane was definitely not carrying parts of a disc and there appears to be no substantiation of a sabotage charge.” The Seattle office closed its investigation in its letter of 18–19 August. No document in the release records a formal finding on the sighting itself.

Reported alternative 1: A story built around ore samples. On 6 August the FBI in Seattle passed on unverified information that “THE ENTIRE STORY STARTED BY DAHL AND CRISMAN POSSIBLY TO PROMOTE SALE OF SLAG FOUND IN A GRAVEL PIT ON MAURY ISLAND”. In their signed statement of 7 August the two men said the flying disc stories “originated over the ore samples which we sent to be analyzed”, and the Seattle office later thought the anonymous telephone calls “were possibly made by FRED CRISMAN in order to build up the flying disc story to the point where they could make a profitable sale of the story to RAY PALMER”.

Reported alternative 2: Slag from a smelter. On 3 August Major Sander of McChord Field compared the fragments left in Arnold’s hotel room with slag at a smelter near Tacoma and, in Smith’s account, “the slag was noted to be definitely similar”; Arnold told the FBI that Sander called them “nothing but slag from the copper mill”. The only other word on the material is a United Press story, reported by the FBI in Portland, that “ANALYSIS OF THE FRAGMENTS SHOWS THEM TO BE FROM A TACOMA SLAG MILL”. No analysis is in the release.

Reported alternative 3: A publisher’s invention. The A-2 officer thought Palmer “might have come across this incident through the University of Chicago”, where Crisman was supposed to have sent samples. The FBI in Chicago, writing on 20 September about Palmer and Richard Shaver, concluded: “It is possible, therefore, that the entire flying disc theory was conceived by PALMER and SHAVER.” That conclusion concerns flying discs in general, not this case alone.

Reported alternative 4: Sabotage of the B-25. This was the claim of an anonymous caller and of the Tacoma Times. The intelligence officers at McChord Field, the A-2 officer there and the FBI found no sabotage; the claim is listed with this case in the claim ledger.

summary.en: From late May 1946 the press in Sweden reported flying missiles, which it named “Ghost Rockets”; in June there were reports from Finland and Denmark, by July from Norway, and by the end of July the Swedish Defense Staff had received almost 1,000. The only account from the time in the US releases is a four-page article in the War Department’s Intelligence Review of 9 January 1947. It records descriptions from “a ball of fire with a tail” to a “shiny cigar-shaped object”, no fragments other than “nonmetallic slag”, and Swedish officers who spoke of Soviet rockets but could produce no evidence. Its authors put the high-altitude reports down to meteors or fireworks and thought that a handful of low-flying ones might have been real missiles.

Lights that followed the aircraft of one night fighter squadron in the winter of 1944–45, as a SHAEF file records them

A file of Air Staff SHAEF in PURSUE release 01 holds 14 extracts from the sortie reports of the 415th Night Fighter Squadron, from ten nights between 14/15 December 1944 and 29/30 January 1945. The crews describe red, orange, yellow, amber, green and white lights, singly, in pairs and in groups, some of which followed their aircraft, one “within 100 ft.” and for “5 minutes”; the squadron called them “Foofighters”. Its intelligence officer wrote: “In every case where pilot called GCI Control and asked if there was a Bogey A/C in the area he received a negative answer.” SHAEF wrote that “it would seem that there must be something more than mere imagination behind the matter”. The Air Ministry suggested Me 262s and flak rockets, and in the same letter: “The whole affair is still something of a mystery”.

Source assessment: Air Staff SHAEF to the First Tactical Air Force, 11 February 1945: “there is no information at this Headquarters which might explain the nature and cause of the lights and other phenomena described by the pilots of this Squadron.” The Air Ministry to SHAEF, 13 March 1945: “A few of the alleged aircraft may have been Me. 262 and for the rest, flak rockets are suggested as the most likely explanation. The whole affair is still something of a mystery and the evidence is very sketchy and varied so that no definite and satisfactory explanation can yet be given.” SHAEF passed the Air Ministry’s view on to the First Tactical Air Force on 18 March: “It is regretted that no further, or more definite, information can be given.”

Reported alternative 1: Me 262 aircraft and flak rockets. The Air Ministry, 13 March 1945: “A few of the alleged aircraft may have been Me. 262 and for the rest, flak rockets are suggested as the most likely explanation.” It does not say which reports it took for aircraft, and in the same letter it adds: “The whole affair is still something of a mystery and the evidence is very sketchy and varied so that no definite and satisfactory explanation can yet be given.”

Reported alternative 2: A “Flak Bombe”. On 17 February 1945 A.D.I.(K) at the Air Ministry wrote that a CX report SHAEF had sent on 14 February “probably refers to ‘Flak Bombe’ mentioned in A.D.I.(K) Report No.562/1944, paragraphs 128 and 129.” Neither the CX report nor that A.D.I.(K) report is in the file, so it is not known what the CX report described or what a “Flak Bombe” was. On 13 March the Air Ministry still called the whole affair “something of a mystery”.

Reported alternative 3: Electrostatic or electromagnetic phenomena, or reflections from ice crystals. What the CIA’s scientific panel heard in January 1953: foo fighters “were believed to be electrostatic (similar to St. Elmo’s fire) or electromagnetic phenomena or possibly light reflections from ice crystals in the air, but their exact cause or nature was never defined.”

A nationwide wave of “mystery airship” sightings half a century before Roswell

For six months American newspapers carried thousands of reports of a cigar-shaped “airship” with searchlights and propellers, crossing the country from California eastward. It is the first mass aerial-anomaly wave in the modern record — and it happened before powered flight existed.
Source assessment: None. No investigative body existed.
Reported alternative 1: Venus and bright stars, at a moment when the press had primed the public to expect an airship.
Reported alternative 2: Deliberate newspaper invention: several reports were later admitted as fabrications by their own editors.
Reported alternative 3: Perceptual templating: the technology of the age — a dirigible with a searchlight — supplied the expected shape.

A broadsheet woodcut describing an “aerial battle” of spheres and crosses above the city. Routinely presented today as evidence of a historical UFO presence — in reality it is a source of an entirely different character from a modern aviation report.
